pedagogy.summary: At age 9-10 pupils identify 3-D shapes — cubes and other cuboids, prisms, pyramids — from 2-D representations: nets, isometric drawings, and other flat pictures. This sits at the demanding interface of 2-D and 3-D: it requires mentally transforming a flat pattern into a closed solid, tracking which faces will meet and which will end up opposite. Research shows the decisive obstacle is that pupils are misled by how a diagram LOOKS — they judge globally ('it looks like a box') rather than reasoning from properties, and this 'look'-driven error persists for years unless taught against. Success depends on coordinating spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating) with explicit domain knowledge (a cube has six square faces; opposite faces never share an edge) — neither alone is enough for anything beyond the simplest case. Effective teaching is hands-on first (cut and fold real nets, build with interlocking pieces), then trains a deliberate strategy: fix a base face, rotate the others up, and anticipate where each face lands — checking the net actually closes with no gaps or overlaps.
bestPractices: Start hands-on: cut out and fold real nets and build solids from interlocking pieces so the fold relationships are concrete before pupils are asked to imagine them
Teach an explicit anticipation strategy — choose a base face, rotate the remaining faces up around it, and predict which faces meet and which become opposite — rather than judging by appearance
Make domain knowledge explicit and usable (a cube has exactly six square faces; opposite faces don't share an edge) so it can coordinate the mental folding
Confront 'look'-driven errors directly with valid vs invalid look-alike nets (same six squares, but one overlaps or leaves a gap) and with shapes drawn in non-standard orientations
Connect net ↔ solid ↔ isometric drawing in both directions: predict the solid from a net, and sketch/point to a net for a given solid
keyRepresentations: Foldable nets (cube, cuboid, triangular prism, square-based pyramid), physical and animated
Isometric drawings of the same solid in different orientations
Valid vs invalid look-alike nets (six squares that do / don't close)
'Choose a base, fold the rest up' anticipation sequence with the opposite-face highlighted
Interlocking construction pieces (e.g. polydron) for building from 2-D faces
commonMisconceptions: Judging the shape by the overall 'look' of the 2-D drawing rather than reasoning from faces/properties
Assuming any arrangement of six squares folds into a cube, without checking it closes without overlaps or gaps
Not anticipating which faces will meet or become opposite — no mental folding, just face-counting
Failing to recognise a solid drawn in a non-standard orientation (prototype/orientation bias)
Treating a flat net as a 2-D shape (its silhouette) rather than a foldable surface of a solid

learn.summary: Pupils aged 9-10 identify 3-D shapes (cubes and other cuboids, prisms, pyramids) from 2-D representations such as nets and isometric drawings. The core challenge is coordinating spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating) with explicit property knowledge (a cube has six square faces; opposite faces never share an edge). The persistent obstacle is 'look'-driven judgement — deciding 'it looks like a box' instead of reasoning from faces and checking a net actually closes. Teaching should start hands-on (cut and fold real nets, build with interlocking pieces) and then train a deliberate anticipation strategy: fix a base face, rotate the others up, and predict which faces meet and which end up opposite.

activities.title: Fold real nets by hand: valid vs look-alike
feedback: If the net closes with no gaps or overlaps you have a valid cube net; if two faces collide or a gap remains, the arrangement cannot be a cube even though it has six squares
When you predicted the opposite face, check after folding: opposite faces never share an edge in the flat net
If a pupil counts 'six squares' and stops, prompt them to fold the look-alike and name exactly which two faces collide

Note that the real paper or card net has a slight thickness and is a close stand-in for the ideal zero-thickness mathematical surface; the reasoning is about the mathematical shape it folds into, not the card itself
activities.rationale: Hands-on cutting, folding and building makes fold relationships concrete, which supports the later mental move; confronting a valid vs invalid six-square pair targets the 'look'-driven error the research identifies.
sourceClaims: Working with 2-D representations of 3-D shapes needs both spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating/drawing nets) and property-based analytic reasoning; for multi-step problems neither alone suffices — the two must be coordinated by explicit domain-specific knowledge to overcome the perceptual 'look' of the diagram, and pupils are frequently misled by how the diagram looks. The difficulty persists across grades 4-9 without targeted teaching, but a single lesson making knowledge explicit produced retained gains.
learnerActions: Cut out and fold a real cube net from paper or card and check it closes with no gaps or overlaps
Fold a look-alike net that has the same six squares but in which two faces overlap or leave a gap, and observe that it refuses to close
Before folding each net, choose a base face and say aloud which face you think will land opposite it, then fold to check
Build a cube-shaped solid and a triangular prism from interlocking construction pieces (e.g. polydron), joining flat faces until the solid closes
activities.intendedInsight: Having six squares is not enough — the arrangement must actually fold into a closed solid. Folding real nets makes the fold relationships concrete before pupils are asked to imagine them.

activities.title: Anticipate the fold: choose a base, rotate the rest up
feedback: If your predicted opposite face is wrong, re-fold slowly and watch which face ends up facing away from the base
If you cannot name which faces meet at an edge, you are counting faces rather than folding — track one face at a time as it rotates up
A correct justification names the base, the meeting faces and the opposite face, not which arrangement 'looks most like a cube'
activities.rationale: Explicit domain knowledge and a deliberate anticipation strategy give pupils something beyond appearance to reason from; an interactive folder that visibly fails to close for invalid nets can make the closure check observable, though it is one optional way to do so rather than a required tool.
sourceClaims: Working with 2-D representations of 3-D shapes needs both spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating/drawing nets) and property-based analytic reasoning; for multi-step problems neither alone suffices — the two must be coordinated by explicit domain-specific knowledge to overcome the perceptual 'look' of the diagram, and pupils are frequently misled by how the diagram looks. The difficulty persists across grades 4-9 without targeted teaching, but a single lesson making knowledge explicit produced retained gains.
learnerActions: Choose a base face on a flat net and state the rule you are using (a cube has exactly six square faces; opposite faces do not share an edge)

Mentally fold each remaining face up along its hinge edge (faces joined to the base first, then the faces joined to those) and predict which faces will meet at each edge and which face lands opposite the base
Write or say your prediction for the finished solid before folding, then fold the real net to check

Optionally, on a controllable folding animation, drag a slider so the faces hinge upward around your chosen base and watch valid nets click shut while invalid ones collide or gap; use the ghost-preview that highlights which face lands opposite the base before folding, and spin the finished solid with a rotate handle
activities.intendedInsight: A reliable method replaces guessing: fix a base, rotate faces up, anticipate which meet and which become opposite, then confirm the net closes.

activities.title: Recognise solids in any orientation and link representations
feedback: If a pupil fails to name a tilted cuboid, ask them to describe the faces they can see and reason about the hidden ones (a cuboid has six rectangular faces in matching opposite pairs) rather than expecting the standard view
Turning a solid does not change what it is — if it has six square faces it is still a cube on whichever face it rests
Linking net <-> solid <-> isometric in both directions checks the connection is understood, not just memorised one way
activities.rationale: Prototype/orientation bias causes pupils to miss familiar solids drawn unusually; identifying by properties across orientations and connecting the representations addresses this. Rotating a solid and watching a net wrap onto it may help make face-adjacency observable that a single flat view can leave implicit; its advantage over hands-on folding is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Upper-KS2 pupils 'identify 3-D shapes, including cubes and other cuboids, from 2-D representations' (e.g. recognising a cuboid from its net or an isometric drawing).

Working with 2-D representations of 3-D shapes needs both spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating/drawing nets) and property-based analytic reasoning; for multi-step problems neither alone suffices — the two must be coordinated by explicit domain-specific knowledge to overcome the perceptual 'look' of the diagram, and pupils are frequently misled by how the diagram looks. The difficulty persists across grades 4-9 without targeted teaching, but a single lesson making knowledge explicit produced retained gains.
learnerActions: Name the 3-D shape shown in isometric drawings of the same solid in several different orientations, including non-standard ones (e.g. a cuboid drawn at an angle or resting on an unfamiliar face)
Justify each name by its faces/properties rather than by matching a single prototypical picture
Go both directions: predict the solid from a given net, and sketch or point to a valid net for a given solid
Optionally use a wrap/unwrap view — fold a net onto a rotatable solid and turn the solid to confirm it is the same shape whichever face it rests on, keeping a flat-net view alongside
activities.intendedInsight: A shape is defined by its faces and properties, so it stays the same shape in any orientation and across net, solid and isometric representations.

activities.title: Diagnostic check: which net folds into a cube?
feedback: Correct: picks the valid net and justifies it by mentally folding — fixing a base, rotating faces up, checking six square faces close with no gaps or overlaps, and naming opposite faces — and rejects the five-face net (missing a face) and the overlapping six-square net (won't close)
Appearance-driven error: picks whichever looks most cube-like or most symmetrical and cannot say which faces meet — make domain knowledge explicit and require a closure check by folding
Six-squares error: accepts the overlapping net 'because it has six squares' and cannot name which faces collide — fold both real look-alike nets so one closes and one fails
Orientation error: fails to name a cuboid drawn at an angle — rotate the object physically and on screen and identify it by its faces across orientations
activities.rationale: A predict-then-fold task with a valid vs invalid six-square pair is diagnostic because the right choice requires mental folding and a closure check, not a glance; stating a reason (which faces meet) exposes whether the pupil reasons from properties or appearance.
sourceClaims: Working with 2-D representations of 3-D shapes needs both spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating/drawing nets) and property-based analytic reasoning; for multi-step problems neither alone suffices — the two must be coordinated by explicit domain-specific knowledge to overcome the perceptual 'look' of the diagram, and pupils are frequently misled by how the diagram looks. The difficulty persists across grades 4-9 without targeted teaching, but a single lesson making knowledge explicit produced retained gains.
learnerActions: Given three flat shapes — one that folds into a closed cube, one missing a face, and one with six squares where two would overlap so it won't close — choose which folds into a cube and explain how you can tell

Answer probe questions: 'Point to the face that ends up opposite this one — how do you know?', 'This also has six squares — why doesn't it make a cube?', 'If I turn the cube onto a different face, is it still a cube? How can you tell?'
Check your answer by cutting and folding the net you chose
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning from properties and mentally folding to check closure distinguishes a genuine understanding from an appearance-based guess.

constraints: Begin hands-on with real cut-and-fold nets and interlocking pieces so fold relationships are concrete before any mental folding is required

A static reference chart (tap a net to reveal its solid and highlight opposite faces) can support recall but does not let a pupil fold a net and watch it close or fail; treat it as a reference, not the main skill-building task

Matching/categorisation items (pick-the-valid-net, name-the-isometric-shape) can check recognition and are useful with look-alike distractors, but recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent mental folding and justification the objective targets; pair them with construction/prediction and a stated reason

Paper and card nets have a real slight thickness and are close approximations of the ideal zero-thickness mathematical surface; a screen folding model is likewise an idealised model — reason about the mathematical solid represented, distinguishing it from the flat picture or physical card

Interactive folding and wrap-onto-solid views are optional ways to make closure and face-adjacency observable; they are examples of the mechanism, not required tools, and should not replace hands-on folding
Include non-standard orientations and valid vs invalid six-square pairs deliberately, since prototype/orientation bias and 'any six squares' assumptions persist without targeted teaching
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Hands-on-first sequencing is drawn from the saved pedagogy summary ('Effective teaching is hands-on first'); the two cited sources establish the look-driven obstacle and the need to coordinate spatial and property reasoning but do not themselves rank hands-on folding above other media.
The source reports that a single explicit-knowledge lesson produced retained gains (Fujita et al. 2020); this is as reported in the cited study and has not been independently re-verified here.

The legacy entry rated a 3-D rotatable model 'strong' and a persona dialogue 'poor' as a visual-spatial fit; these are retained as narrow pedagogical observations, not as universal claims that one medium is necessary, better, or that dialogue cannot contribute.

The legacy phrasing that an interactive folder 'directly attacks' the misconception, and that a 3-D wrap view conveys what a flat view cannot, is softened: observable failure-to-close and wrap-on-solid views may help confront the error and surface face-adjacency, but comparative efficacy over hands-on folding is not established by the sources here.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a flat net and ask them to PREDICT which 3-D shape it will fold into, and to point out which two faces will end up opposite each other — BEFORE folding. Then cut and fold it to check. The prediction and the stated reason (which faces meet) are the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Point to the face that will end up OPPOSITE this one when it's folded — how do you know they become opposite?
This one also has six squares — why doesn't it make a cube?
If I turn the cube to sit on a different face, is it still a cube? How can you tell?
Fold it in your head: which two faces meet at this edge?
assess.correctAnswer: Picks the valid cube net and justifies it by mentally folding — fixing a base face, rotating the others up, and checking that six square faces close with no gaps or overlaps (and which faces end up opposite) — rather than by which arrangement 'looks most like a cube'. Correctly rejects the five-face net (a face is missing) and the overlapping six-square net (it won't close).

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by the overall 'look' of the arrangement rather than reasoning from faces — picks whichever looks most cube-like or most symmetrical
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make domain knowledge explicit (a cube has six square faces; opposite faces don't share an edge) and require mental folding/closure checking rather than a visual judgement
errorPatterns.distractor: The one that looks most like a cube / is most symmetrical.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses a net by appearance and cannot say which faces meet, or is swayed by symmetry over closure

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes any six squares fold into a cube — counts faces without anticipating which meet or checking the net closes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the anticipation strategy — choose a base, rotate faces up, predict which faces meet — and fold real look-alike nets to see one close and one fail
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the overlapping six-square net as a cube 'because it has six squares', and cannot name which faces would collide

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot recognise a solid drawn or resting in a non-standard orientation (prototype/orientation bias)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the object physically and on screen; identify it by its faces/properties across orientations, not by a single prototypical picture
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fails to name a cuboid drawn at an angle or a shape lying on an unfamiliar face, expecting only the 'standard' view

responseLevels.gap: Judges by overall appearance, treats any six-square arrangement as a cube, and cannot say which faces meet.
responseLevels.full: Determines the solid by mentally folding — fixing a base, rotating faces up, checking the net closes with no gaps or overlaps and which faces become opposite — using explicit properties, and recognises the shape in any orientation or representation.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies standard nets and drawings of familiar shapes and counts faces, but is misled by an invalid look-alike net or a non-standard orientation — recognises the parts without anticipating how they fold together.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three flat shapes in front of the child: one folds into a closed cube, one is missing a face, and one has six squares but two would overlap so it won't close. Say: 'Which one folds into a cube? Explain how you can tell.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reasons from properties folds mentally and checks closure, choosing the valid net and rejecting the overlapping look-alike; a child driven by appearance picks the most cube-looking arrangement or counts 'six squares' without checking they close. The valid vs invalid six-square pair is the trap — the right choice needs mental folding, not a glance.
